summary: Describes active tail extensions to Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) for multipoint networks. These let the receiving ends of a multipoint path take a more active part, such as telling the sender about their state. It builds on the multipoint BFD work and is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: In a group check where one person calls out, this lets listeners answer back too, so the caller knows who can hear.

questions: what is bfd multipoint active tail
what is an m-poll in bfd
subtitle: How the listeners on a multipoint path can tell the sender when they lose its packets.

tldr.problem: In multipoint BFD the head sends to many tails, but the head never learns which tails have lost connectivity. Letting every tail talk back risks overwhelming the head.
tldr.mechanism: Tails can send unicast BFD Control packets to the head when the multipoint path fails. The head stays in control of timing, and it can solicit replies with a multipoint Poll or check one tail with a unicast Poll Sequence.
tldr.outcome: The head can learn reasonably quickly which tails lost connectivity, and it can silence all tails, or chosen ones, when it does not want to hear from them.

facts.label: Rate with no head notification
facts.value: At most one BFD packet per second

today: RFC 8563 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2019. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata, and it builds on RFC 8562.

sections.title: Why Tails Need to Speak
sections.content:
RFC 8563 extends Multipoint BFD from RFC 8562. In that base design one sender, the head, sends BFD Control packets to many receivers, the tails. Here, multipoint means any mechanism where one or more systems receive packets sent by a single sender, such as IP multicast and point-to-multipoint MPLS.

The extension lets tails notify the head when they lose multipoint connectivity. The goal is that the head quickly knows which tails have lost connectivity from it. Scaling is the main worry, particularly state explosion toward the head. So the head MUST control all timing, and the BFD packets from tails to the head must not be synchronized.

The document effectively modifies and adds to Sections 5.12 and 5.13 of RFC 8562.
sections.eli5: The sender wants to know which listeners can no longer hear it. But if all of them shout at once, it gets drowned out, so the sender sets the rules.

sections.title: Three Ways to Learn About Tails
sections.content:
The head has several options. First, for a best-effort failure notification, tails can send unsolicited unicast BFD Control packets to the head when the path fails.

Second, the head can send a multipoint BFD Control packet with the Poll (P) bit set. Tails answer with a unicast BFD Control packet with the Final (F) bit set. The RFC calls this the Multipoint Poll (m-poll). Tails that stop answering are likely to have lost connectivity.

Third, if a tail missed the last m-poll, the head can start a Demand mode Poll Sequence by unicast to that tail. Combining multipoint and unicast polling is called the Composite Poll (c-poll). The head may also poll a subset of important tails on their own schedule.

Individual tails can also be configured never to send BFD Control packets to the head. The head never learns of them, but they still detect multipoint path failures themselves.
sections.eli5: The sender can wait for listeners to speak up, call out 'who is there?' to everyone, or knock on one listener's door to check. Some listeners can choose to stay quiet.

sections.title: Operational Scenarios
sections.content:
Three paths matter: the multipoint path, the forward unicast path (head to tail) and the reverse unicast path (tail to head). The RFC walks through what the head can and cannot know when each one fails.

With no head notification, only the multipoint path is used. The tail notices a failure within a Detection Time and the head stays ignorant. This mimics RFC 8562. bfd.SilentTail MUST be 1 on the tail, and bfd.ReportTailDown MUST be zero on the head.

With head notification, bfd.SilentTail MUST be zero on tails, bfd.ReportTailDown MUST be 1 on the head, and the head MUST set bfd.RequiredMinRxInterval to nonzero. If the multipoint path fails but the reverse unicast path works, the head learns within one reverse packet time. If both fail, the tail detects the failure but the head cannot know.

If only the reverse unicast path fails, the head sees the BFD session fail but cannot tell the state of the multipoint path, and the tail keeps receiving multipoint data.

A Down or AdminDown packet from a tail reliably tells the head that multipoint connectivity was lost. A silent tail is ambiguous, because the cause could be the multipoint path or either unicast path.
sections.eli5: If the sender hears 'I can't hear you', it knows. If it hears nothing, it can't tell whether the listener is gone or the phone line back is broken.

sections.title: New State Variables and Session Type
sections.content:
The RFC adds a session type, MultipointClient, to bfd.SessionType. It is a session on the head that tracks one individual tail. All client sessions for a multipoint path are associated with the MultipointHead session. They receive packets from tails and MUST NOT send periodic BFD Control packets other than Poll Sequences. Settings in a client session override those in the head session.

  • bfd.SilentTail: if 1, the tail never sends packets to the head. The default MUST be 1. It applies to MultipointTail sessions.
  • bfd.ReportTailDown: if 1, the head wants tails to send periodic BFD Control packets when they see the session fail. The default MUST be zero.
  • bfd.UnicastRcvd: set to 1 when a tail in Up state receives a unicast BFD Control packet from the head; MUST be initialized to zero.

For client sessions, bfd.LocalDiscr, bfd.DesiredMinTxInterval and bfd.DetectMult MUST always match the head session. bfd.DemandMode MUST be initialized to 1. The head may set bfd.RequiredMinRxInterval to zero to suppress tail traffic, for all tails or a single tail.
sections.eli5: The sender gets a notebook page for each listener it cares about, plus a few switches that say whether listeners may speak up.

sections.title: Polling, Replies and Detection Times
sections.content:
Because the fan-in from tails could be very large, tail traffic must be controlled. The head always operates in Demand mode, so no tail sends asynchronous packets while the session is Up. A Required Min Rx Interval received in a unicast packet takes precedence over one received in multipoint packets.

To solicit tails, the head sends a multipoint BFD Control packet with the Poll bit set to 1. Tails reply by unicast, randomized across one packet interval. A multipoint Poll MUST NOT be sent more often than the regular multipoint BFD Control packet. The Detection Time, equal to bfd.DesiredMinTxInterval, MUST be greater than the round-trip time from head to tail and back.

To verify one tail, a client session sends a Poll Sequence by unicast. The value it carries in Required Min RX Interval is then used by that tail, and the tail's reply is not delayed. This is 'sticky': to undo it, the head SHOULD send a Poll Sequence with the same value as in the multipoint packets, or MAY reset the tail with a Poll Sequence with state AdminDown.

A tail sending its first periodic packet delays it by a random time between zero and (0.9 * bfd.RemoteMinRxInterval), which avoids synchronized replies. On the head, packets from tails are demultiplexed by source address and Your Discriminator together, since all tails echo the same discriminator.
sections.eli5: When the sender calls 'who is there?', each listener waits a random moment before answering, so they do not all talk at once. Knocking on one door gets a faster answer.

sections.title: Assumptions and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Head notification assumes the multipoint encapsulation holds enough information for a tail to address a unicast BFD packet to the head, and that bidirectional unicast communication exists between tail and head. For the head to know reliably that a tail lost multipoint connectivity, both unicast paths must stay up when the multipoint path fails, so they should not share fate with it where possible. Because the normal BFD three-way handshake is not used, a tail that goes Up to Down and back to Up may not be reliably detected at the head.

The congestion control requirements of RFC 5880 Section 7 also apply. With no head notifications, the head MUST limit transmission to no more than one BFD packet per second.
sections.eli5: This only works if the listener has a working way to call back. If the sender can only be heard on a broken line, it stays in the dark.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content: The security considerations of RFC 5880 and RFC 8562 apply. In addition, implementations that create MultipointClient sessions dynamically on receipt of a tail's packet MUST protect against the number of such sessions growing out of control. The RFC suggests raising an alarm when the count exceeds the number of expected tails, and keeping a reasonable upper bound, possibly based on the number of multicast streams expected. This document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: If anyone could add themselves to the sender's notebook, the notebook could fill up. So the sender must set a limit and sound an alarm.

messages.label: Multipoint BFD Control (P=1)
messages.note: Sent over the multipoint path to all tails.

messages.label: Unicast BFD Control (F=1)
messages.note: Reply delayed by a random amount.

messages.label: Unicast Poll Sequence
messages.note: Sent if a tail did not answer the multipoint Poll.

messages.label: BFD Control (F=1)
messages.note: Not delayed; carries the tail's session state.
